editorial.title: The New Supply Chain Risk Is Dependency
editorial.dek: The real resilience question is no longer how much capacity exists, but how many practical ways cargo can move when preferred routes stop behaving normally.
body: The question, “How much capacity is available?” is becoming increasingly irrelevant.

This week alone, logistics networks were dealing with severe port congestion in East Asia, new operational pressure around the Strait of Hormuz, and further restrictions at the Panama Canal. None of these situations mean the world has suddenly run out of ships, terminals, trucks or infrastructure. The problem is that too much cargo still depends on a relatively small number of routes, gateways and operating assumptions.

At Shanghai and Ningbo, successive typhoons have created vessel queues stretching several days. Global containership capacity waiting to berth reached about 4.31 million TEU, with Shanghai waiting times reported as high as 12 days at some terminals. A leading carrier has already omitted Shanghai calls on certain voyages to protect onward schedules.

With this year’s lower-than-expected rainfall, the Panama Canal Authority announced reduced daily transit capacity beginning in September. It has also been adjusting draft restrictions and its booking system as water conditions change. Access to the Canal is becoming more conditional, particularly for vessels without secured reservations.
Then there is the Strait of Hormuz. This week, Iran threatened penalties, detention and possible cargo confiscation against dozens of tankers it says violated its transit requirements.
One is weather. One is water availability. One is geopolitics.
Operationally, however, they expose the same weakness.
Supply chains that run efficiently through preferred routes are often much less efficient when those routes stop behaving normally.
That changes how resilience should be measured.

A company may have three carriers, but if all three depend on the same transshipment hub, the diversification is mostly cosmetic. A shipper may have several suppliers, but if all of them export through the same congested gateway, the risk remains concentrated. If alternatives only become visible after the primary routing fails, they are contingency plans rather than real options.
How much capacity do you have?
How many practical ways do you have to move your cargo?
That means looking beyond freight rates and transit times when planning important shipments.
Efficiency matters. None of this means abandoning it.
But the cheapest or fastest routing on a normal day is not necessarily the lowest-cost routing across the life of a shipment.
A supply chain with one perfect route is efficient. A supply chain with three workable routes is resilient.

items.title: Etihad Rail and AD Ports launch Fujairah–ICAD freight corridor with inland customs clearance
items.discovery: Middle East rail-freight, port-gateway and customs-infrastructure scan; checked against Etihad Rail network information
items.summary: Etihad Rail and AD Ports Group launched a three-times-weekly freight service linking Fujairah Terminals with ICAD in Abu Dhabi. Containers can move about 200 km by rail to the customs-enabled inland gateway, which now has its own UN LOCODE, AECAD, allowing cargo to be booked directly there for inspection, clearance and release.
items.logisticsImpact: The service gives importers an inland clearance option tied directly to an East Coast port outside the Strait of Hormuz. It can shift high-volume cargo from long-haul trucking to rail, reduce handling at the port and strengthen Fujairah as an alternative gateway for Abu Dhabi industry.

items.title: Gulf producers expand tanker shuttle and ship-to-ship system to keep oil moving through Hormuz disruption
items.discovery: Gulf tanker-routing, energy-logistics and Hormuz workaround scan; cross-checked against Reuters vessel-flow reporting
items.region: Strait of Hormuz / Oman / Middle East / Asia
items.summary: Gulf producers are increasingly using shuttle tankers to move crude through exposed Gulf waters and transfer it ship-to-ship off Oman to larger vessels for onward voyages. Reuters reports the workaround has helped lift exports through Hormuz to about 6.5 million barrels per day, but freight costs on affected movements have climbed above $30 per barrel.
items.logisticsImpact: The shuttle model keeps export volumes moving but consumes extra tanker capacity, adds marine handling and lengthens vessel cycles. Wider adoption by Gulf producers tightens VLCC availability and can raise tanker rates well beyond the immediate Hormuz trade.

items.title: Trafigura launches Volare Shipping with 14-VLCC fleet plan
items.discovery: Global tanker-capacity and energy-shipping scan; cross-checked with Reuters and Lloyd's List
items.summary: Trafigura has created Volare Shipping with six VLCCs already operating and eight newbuildings scheduled for delivery through 2028. The company plans to raise about $500 million and list the tanker business in Oslo, with the proceeds funding the current newbuilding programme.
items.logisticsImpact: The move adds a dedicated owner-backed fleet platform to a tanker market strained by longer routes and Gulf disruption. Bringing eight additional modern VLCCs into the fleet through 2028 increases future crude-transport capacity while giving Trafigura greater control over freight exposure.

items.title: Pepco opens Gdańsk-area distribution hub and locks in longer container contracts
items.discovery: European retail logistics, warehousing and ocean-contracting scan; cross-checked against Pepco Group facility information
items.summary: Pepco has opened a new distribution centre near Gdańsk as it responds to unreliable ocean schedules and higher freight costs. The site will support roughly 400 stores and is designed to deconsolidate imports arriving through Gdańsk and Gdynia, while Pepco has secured container contracts extending beyond next summer.
items.logisticsImpact: The hub moves import allocation closer to Poland’s Baltic gateways and gives Pepco more control over deconsolidation and store replenishment. Longer freight contracts reduce exposure to spot-rate spikes, while the facility can shorten inland movements and improve routing flexibility for Northern and Central Europe.
